beats.vo: Every single day, you are being argued with. By the news, by adverts, by that one relative at dinner, by strangers online, by your own anxious thoughts at 2 AM. And a huge amount of it is quietly, cleverly, wrong. Not lying exactly, but broken, flawed reasoning, dressed up to look completely convincing.
beats.title: EVERY LOGICAL FALLACY
beats.subtitle: the tricks that fool your logic

beats.vo: These are logical fallacies, and once you can see them, you genuinely cannot unsee them. They're everywhere. In the comment section, in the sales pitch, in the political speech. Learning them is like getting a pair of glasses that reveals the hidden tricks in almost every argument around you.

But first, what even is an argument? Not a shouting match. It's a claim, held up by legs of evidence and reasoning. A good argument stands because its legs are solid. A fallacy is a sneaky way to make a claim look like it's standing, when really, it has no legs underneath it at all.

Welcome to Dear Brain. Twelve of the most common logical fallacies, the ones hiding in your feed, your arguments, and even your own head. For each, we'll name it, show you a vivid example, and give you the one simple move that defuses it. Let's go.

Here is our rogues' gallery. Twelve ways an argument can trick you. Some attack the wrong target, some offer fake choices, and some just tug at your heart until you quietly stop thinking altogether. See how many you recognise from the very last conversation you had online.

Number one, and the most common of them all. The strawman. Instead of arguing against what someone actually said, you quietly swap it for a weaker, sillier version, a man made of straw, then triumphantly knock that down. I think we should fund more parks. Oh, so you want to bankrupt the entire country?
beats.title: 1 — THE STRAWMAN
beats.subtitle: attacking a fake version

beats.vo: It feels like a crushing victory, but you never actually touched their real point. You just built a flimsy dummy and set it on fire. It's so common because it's so easy. A distorted, extreme version of someone's view is always simpler to attack than the careful, reasonable thing they really said.

The counter? Steelman instead. Before you respond, restate their argument so fairly and so strongly that they'd nod and say, yes, exactly that. Then reply to that. If their point sounds absurd in your retelling, you're probably arguing with straw. Beat their best case, not their worst.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number two. The ad hominem, Latin for, to the person. When you can't beat the argument, you attack the arguer instead. Well, of course you'd say that, you didn't even go to college. What would you know, you're broke. Notice it dodges the point entirely, and just slings mud at the human holding it.
beats.title: 2 — AD HOMINEM
beats.subtitle: attack the person, not the point

beats.vo: Here is the rule that beats it every time. In any argument, play the ball, not the player. The ball is the idea, which is true or false entirely on its own. Who happens to be holding it, whether you like them, whether they're even a hypocrite, is completely beside the point.

So when someone comes at you personally, don't take the bait and defend yourself. Gently steer back. You might be right about me, but let's stick to the actual argument. A genius and a fool can both say the sky is blue, and the sky is blue either way.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number three. The slippery slope. The claim that one small, reasonable step must inevitably trigger a chain reaction, sliding all the way down to total disaster. If we let students redo one test, next they'll expect to redo everything, and soon no one will ever learn anything, ever again.
beats.title: 3 — SLIPPERY SLOPE
beats.subtitle: one step to catastrophe

beats.vo: Each step down the slope needs its own evidence, and usually there just isn't any. The argument simply assumes the very worst outcome at every single link in the chain. But one small, sensible change does not automatically doom us to the bottom of the hill. Fear is doing all the work here, not logic.

To counter it, inspect each step on its own. Ask, is this link actually likely, and what would stop it? Most slopes have plenty of footholds, rules, limits, common sense, that halt the slide long before the catastrophe. Demand the evidence for the fall, not just the vivid, scary picture of it.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number four. The false dilemma. You're handed just two options, usually one terrible and one they're selling, when in reality there are many more. You're either with us, or you're against us. Love it or leave it. The whole trick is quietly hiding every other door in the room.
beats.title: 4 — FALSE DILEMMA
beats.subtitle: only two choices?

beats.vo: It's powerful because it feels so clean and decisive, and because fear and urgency make us crave simple choices. But real life almost always has a third door, and a fourth, and a messy, reasonable maybe somewhere in between the two loud extremes they're offering you.

The counter is a single, calm question. Are those really the only two options? Just naming the hidden third door often collapses the whole trap. Why not some of both? Why not a different path entirely? Refuse to be squeezed into someone else's convenient little box of two.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number five. The appeal to authority. Treating something as true purely because an important-sounding person said it. A celebrity endorses a supplement. A confident voice says, trust me, I'm a doctor, about something far outside their actual field. The crown does all the arguing, instead of the evidence.
beats.title: 5 — APPEAL TO AUTHORITY
beats.subtitle: 'because they said so'

beats.vo: One very fair caveat here. Trusting a real expert, speaking inside their real field, is sensible, not a fallacy. We can't all personally test everything. The flaw is only when authority replaces evidence, or when the expert is confidently talking miles outside their actual lane.

So the counter is two quick questions. Are they genuinely qualified on this specific thing? And what's the actual evidence they're pointing to, underneath the title? A real expert can show you their reasoning. Someone just waving a crown usually can't. Follow the evidence, not the costume.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number six. The bandwagon. It must be true, because everybody believes it. Everyone's buying this, so it has to be good. Millions of people can't all be wrong. It feels safe and warm to follow the crowd, so this one slips past our guard almost constantly.
beats.title: 6 — THE BANDWAGON
beats.subtitle: 'everyone thinks so'

beats.vo: But popularity is simply not proof. Huge numbers of people have believed completely false things all through history, confidently, for centuries. How many people agree with an idea tells you what's currently fashionable, or well-marketed, but it tells you almost nothing about what's actually true.

The counter is to quietly step off the wagon and ask, forget the crowd, what's the actual evidence here? Some of history's most important truths started as deeply unpopular opinions held by a tiny minority. The real question is never who else believes this. It's always, is it true?
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number seven. The red herring. A distraction, something irrelevant dragged noisily across the trail to pull you off the scent. You ask a politician a hard question about rising prices, and suddenly they're passionately talking about the flag, or their opponent. The original question quietly disappears.
beats.title: 7 — THE RED HERRING
beats.subtitle: a shiny distraction

beats.vo: The red herring wins by changing the subject so smoothly that you forget what you were even asking. It often comes wrapped in something emotional or outrageous, precisely because strong feelings make a brilliant distraction from a question someone would rather not answer.

The defence is simple but surprisingly powerful. Just notice the swerve, and gently, politely, steer right back. That's interesting, but it doesn't answer my question. So, back to the prices. Refuse to chase the fish. Keep calmly returning to the point they're trying so hard to avoid.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number eight. Circular reasoning. The argument that quietly assumes the very thing it's supposed to prove, going round and round. This rule is correct, because it's the rule. He's trustworthy, because he says he's trustworthy. The conclusion is just hiding, in disguise, inside the premise.
beats.title: 8 — CIRCULAR REASONING
beats.subtitle: true because it's true

beats.vo: It sounds like a reason, it has the shape of a reason, but it never actually leaves the starting point. No new, independent evidence ever gets to enter the loop. It's a sentence chasing its own tail, forever, and hoping you're too dizzy watching to notice it never arrives anywhere.

To break it, ask one question. But how do we know that first part is true? If the only answer they can give circles straight back to the conclusion, you've found the trap. Push for an outside reason, a fact, a source, anything from beyond the circle. If none exists, the argument is empty.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number nine. The hasty generalisation. Taking one or two vivid examples and stamping them onto absolutely everyone. I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there is rude. My grandad smoked and lived to ninety, so smoking's clearly fine. A tiny sample, treated as the whole, entire truth.
beats.title: 9 — HASTY GENERALISATION
beats.subtitle: one example, big conclusion

beats.vo: A few striking cases feel incredibly convincing, because stories stick in the mind far better than statistics. But they're nowhere near enough to support a sweeping rule. This is the quiet engine behind a huge amount of prejudice and stereotyping, the single bad example, promoted to a universal law.

The counter is to ask, how big and how fair is this sample, really? A couple of memorable stories is an anecdote, not evidence about millions of people. Watch especially for words like all, always, everyone, and none. Reality is almost always messier, and far more varied, than that.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number ten. The appeal to emotion. Skipping logic entirely and going straight for your feelings, fear, pity, pride, outrage, to win you over. Think of the children. If you really cared, you would agree with me. The whole goal is to make you feel so much, so fast, that you simply stop thinking.
beats.title: 10 — APPEAL TO EMOTION
beats.subtitle: feelings instead of reasons

beats.vo: To be fair, emotions are absolutely not the enemy here. The best causes in the world should move us deeply, and a heart untouched by suffering isn't noble, it's just cold. The fallacy is only when a feeling is used instead of a reason, not alongside one. Emotion plus evidence, good. Emotion as evidence, dangerous.

So when a message floods you with strong feeling, pause, take a breath, and ask the quiet question underneath. Setting the feelings aside for just a second, is there actually an argument in here? If every drop of the persuasion is emotional and none of it is factual, be very, very careful.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number eleven. The tu quoque, or, you too. Deflecting a criticism by flinging it straight back, instead of actually answering it. A parent says, you really shouldn't smoke. The teen fires back, well, you smoke! Which may be perfectly true, but it does absolutely nothing to make smoking good for either of them.
beats.title: 11 — TU QUOQUE
beats.subtitle: 'well, you do it too!'

beats.vo: Pointing out hypocrisy can feel like an absolute knockout blow, and it's deeply satisfying. But it's a dodge, pure and simple. Whether the other person practises what they preach has no bearing whatsoever on whether their actual point is correct. A hypocrite can still be completely, annoyingly right.

The counter is to separate the two questions. You might be a hypocrite, and your advice might still be good. Both can be true at once. So you can say, fair enough, I should take my own advice too, and then calmly return to whether the point itself actually holds up.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: Number twelve. The false cause. Seeing two things happen together, or one after the other, and assuming one must have caused the other. The rooster crows, then the sun rises, so the rooster must summon the dawn. I wore my lucky socks, and we won, so the socks did it. Correlation, mistaken for cause.
beats.title: 12 — FALSE CAUSE
beats.subtitle: correlation isn't cause

beats.vo: Two things can rise and fall together for all sorts of reasons. Pure coincidence. Or, very often, some third hidden cause quietly driving both of them at once. Ice cream sales and drowning rates climb together, but ice cream isn't the culprit. It's summer, heating up both at the same time.

So before you ever connect two dots into a cause, ask, could this just be coincidence? Or is something else driving both? Just because B follows A does not mean A caused B. This one quietly fuels superstitions, bad science, and a thousand wrong conclusions. Demand a real mechanism, not just a pattern.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: So how do you armour yourself against all twelve at once? You don't need to memorise the Latin names, or carry a checklist to dinner. You just need a few quick red flags. When an argument starts to feel slippery or off, run this little mental scan, and the trick usually jumps right out at you.

Is this argument attacking a person instead of the point? Forcing me into only two options? Flooding me with emotion? Or quietly dodging the actual question? If the answer to any of those is yes, slow right down. You've probably just caught a fallacy, mid-flight, before it could fool you.
beats.title: BUILD YOUR SHIELD
beats.subtitle: spot them in the wild

beats.vo: And turn that same lens on yourself, gently. We all reach for these tricks, especially when we're losing, or scared, or emotional. The goal of all this isn't to become the insufferable person who shouts fallacy in every conversation. It's to think a little more clearly, and argue a little more honestly.

One last, genuinely important note. Spotting a fallacy means the argument was weak, not that the conclusion is automatically false. Even a terribly argued point can happen to be completely true. Pointing at a bad argument and shouting, therefore you're wrong, is actually its own little fallacy.
beats.subject: face

beats.vo: So use these twelve as a shield, not a sword. Not to win fights and dunk on strangers, but to protect your own mind from being fooled, and to build arguments so clean and fair that you'd be proud to have them used right back on you. That's the real prize here.

Tell me in the comments which fallacy you see the most out in the wild. I'm betting on the strawman. Thank you so much for thinking this through with me today. I'm Dear Brain. Go forth, spot the tricks, and reason well out there.
beats.subject: face
